evals.query: Our CEO wants to add a social feed to our language-learning app: learners post their progress, follow friends and comment. The CEO thinks it will fix retention (30-day retention is 18%). Engineering estimates three months. I'm the PM. Should we build it?
expected_behavior: Gives a clear position early (build, do not build, or test first) rather than only a list of considerations.
Reframes the request around the underlying problem (why learners stop before day 30) and says what evidence would show a feed addresses it.
Offers at least two alternative approaches to the retention problem besides a full feed (for example study partners, lightweight sharing, better streak recovery).
Covers risks beyond whether people want it: whether they can use it, the cost to build and run it (including moderation, and privacy for learners who may be minors), and whether it fits the business.
Proposes a cheap test that takes days or weeks rather than the three-month build, with a stated pass or fail threshold.
Separates what is known (18% retention) from what is assumed (that social features drive retention for these learners).

evals.query: Shared lists in our grocery list app have been flat for six months: about 9% of active households use them, and two redesigns of the sharing screen didn't move it. The team is tired of it. What should we do next?
expected_behavior: Opens with a recommendation for the next step.

Questions whether the sharing screen is the real problem and offers specific hypotheses about why households don't share (for example one person does all the shopping, households already coordinate in a messaging app, the invited person never installs the app).
Proposes learning from real households before another redesign (for example talking to sharing and non-sharing households, or measuring each step of the invite funnel).
Lays out two or three distinct directions, including stopping or parking the feature as a real option.
Gives the recommended next step a time box and a pass mark that decides whether to continue.
Distinguishes what the 9% figure shows from what it does not (for example whether sharing households retain better or shop more).
